name: Robert Kahn
teaser: American computer scientist who, with Vint Cerf, designed the TCP/IP protocols — the plumbing of the internet — in 1973–74, and demonstrated the first internet (connecting different networks) in 1977. He received the 2004 Turing Award, and his design principle — a network of networks that doesn't care what's inside — built the modern world.

exploreAction.targetName: Kahn & Cerf's 1974 paper 'A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication'
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Kahn, working at DARPA, wanted networks to interoperate, and with Cerf invented a protocol that treats every network as a black box, passing packets through a 'gateway.' The 1977 demo linked three networks across a moving truck. Their design deliberately had no central control — which is why the internet survived the decades and why no one owns it.

name: J. C. R. Licklider
teaser: American psychologist and computer scientist who envisioned the 'Intergalactic Computer Network' in 1963 — the idea that became the internet — and the human-computer symbiosis that became personal computing. As DARPA's first computing director, he funded the research that built both the internet and interactive computing.

exploreAction.targetName: Licklider's 1960 paper 'Man-Computer Symbiosis' and his 1963 memos
exploreAction.instruction: Read his 1960 paper, which imagined people and computers working together in real time — then radical. His 1963 memo about an 'Intergalactic Computer Network' is the internet's founding document. He funded time-sharing, graphics, and networking researchers, including the team that built ARPANET. Most of the internet's founders credit him as the grandfather.

name: Douglas Engelbart
teaser: American engineer who, in 1968, gave the 'Mother of All Demos' — introducing the computer mouse, hypertext, windows, video conferencing, and collaborative editing, live on stage. The demo was so far ahead of its time that most of the audience didn't grasp what they'd seen. He believed computers should augment human intelligence, not just calculate.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Engelbart's lab at SRI built the oN-Line System (NLS) — a computer where text, links, and graphics lived together, controlled by a mouse he invented (patented in 1967, never profiting). The 90-minute demo showed video calls and real-time document editing 15 years before the PC. The mouse he designed took 20 more years to become standard.

name: Alan Kay
teaser: American computer scientist who invented the idea of the personal computer — he imagined a 'Dynabook,' a laptop for children, in 1968 — and led the Xerox PARC team that built the Alto, the first computer with a graphical interface, windows, and mouse, in 1973. Steve Jobs saw the Alto and built the Macintosh from its ideas. Kay won the 2003 Turing Award.

exploreAction.targetName: Kay's 1972 Dynabook paper and the Xerox Alto
exploreAction.instruction: Read Kay's vision: a computer as a personal, portable, programmable tool for thought — a 'Dynabook' — years before laptops existed. The Alto he built at PARC ran Smalltalk, the first object-oriented language, with a mouse and bitmapped screen. Jobs' 1979 visit to PARC famously 'changed everything' at Apple. Kay's line: 'The best way to predict the future is to invent it.'

name: Dennis Ritchie
teaser: American computer scientist who created the C programming language and, with Ken Thompson, built the UNIX operating system at Bell Labs in the early 1970s. C and UNIX became the foundation of modern computing: Linux, macOS, Android, and iOS all descend from them. He won the 1983 Turing Award and the 2011 National Medal of Technology.

exploreAction.targetName: Ritchie & Thompson's 1974 paper 'The UNIX Time-Sharing System'
exploreAction.instruction: Read how UNIX was designed as a small system where 'everything is a file' and programs do one thing well — a philosophy that still shapes software. Ritchie's C language was a thin layer over the machine, powerful enough to write operating systems. He was famously modest: asked what his proudest achievement was, he replied, 'The UNIX operating system.'

name: Richard Stallman
teaser: American programmer who launched the free software movement in 1983 with the GNU project, wrote the GNU General Public License, and built the tools — compilers, editors, and the free operating system — that became the GNU/Linux stack running most of the world's servers and Android phones. He coined 'copyleft.'

exploreAction.instruction: Read the manifesto, which argues that software should be free — free as in freedom, not price: the right to use, study, share, and improve. Stallman left MIT to build GNU full-time, writing the Emacs editor and GCC compiler. The license he wrote, GPL, uses copyright to guarantee those freedoms forever. Linux joined GNU in 1991, and the pair now power the internet.

name: Linus Torvalds
teaser: Finnish-American software engineer who, as a 21-year-old student in 1991, wrote the Linux kernel and released it free on the internet — and today it runs most of the world's servers, the majority of cloud computing, every Android phone, and much of the web. He also created Git, the version-control system used by nearly all software projects, and said, 'Talk is cheap. Show me the code.'

exploreAction.instruction: Read the modest post: 'Hello everybody out there using minix — I'm doing a (free) operating system (just a hobby, won't be big and professional like gnu).' Linux became the world's largest collaborative project, with thousands of developers. Torvalds wrote Git in 2005 after frustration with existing tools; it now hosts the code of almost every company on Earth.

name: Larry Page
teaser: American computer scientist who, with Sergey Brin, built Google in 1998 from a Stanford research project — PageRank, which ranks web pages by how many other pages link to them. Google grew to organize the world's information, and Page served as Alphabet's CEO. He is also an early investor in flying-car and asteroid-mining ventures.

exploreAction.targetName: Page & Brin's 1998 paper 'The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine'
exploreAction.instruction: Read the paper: while other search engines counted keyword matches, PageRank treated every link as a vote — a page is important if important pages link to it, computed like a Markov chain. The idea beat the incumbents (AltaVista, Yahoo) and made Google the web's front door. The paper's title, 'anatomy of a search engine,' became the blueprint for the information economy.

name: Steve Wozniak
teaser: American engineer who single-handedly designed the Apple I and Apple II — the computers that launched the personal computer industry in 1976–77. Working at night with minimal chips, he built a machine that a family could use, and his Apple II became the most successful early PC. He is remembered for engineering elegance over commerce.

exploreAction.targetName: Wozniak's design of the Apple I and Apple II
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Wozniak, an HP employee building computers as a hobby, hand-wrote the Apple I on paper, then the Apple II — with color graphics, sound, and expansion slots, years ahead of rivals. Jobs, his friend, handled the business. Wozniak designed the machines so carefully that his BASIC interpreter ran on 4 KB of RAM. He said he wanted 'a computer that people could use.'

name: Herman Hollerith
teaser: American inventor who built the first electric tabulating machine — reading data from punched cards — to process the 1890 U.S. Census in one year instead of the eight the 1880 census had taken. His company, the Tabulating Machine Company, later became IBM. The punched card he invented dominated computing for a century.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Hollerith, a census clerk, mechanized data processing: holes in cards representing age, sex, and occupation, read by electrical contacts, feeding counters. The census of 63 million people was tabulated in about two and a half years, saving $5 million. His cards and machines became the standard for data processing until the 1960s, when IBM's 80-column card — still called a 'Hollerith card' — was everywhere.

name: William Shockley
teaser: American physicist who led the team that invented the transistor at Bell Labs in 1947, sharing the 1956 Nobel. He later moved to Silicon Valley and founded the company that became Intel — but his reputation was destroyed by his public advocacy of eugenics, and he died estranged from the industry he created.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Bardeen and Brattain built the first working transistor in December 1947, and how Shockley, their boss, took charge and followed with the more practical junction transistor. Shockley's personality drove Bardeen to leave, but his Silicon Valley lab trained the 'Traitorous Eight' who founded Fairchild and Intel. His later racist and eugenic views made him a pariah — a complicated legacy for a giant of science.

name: Jack Kilby
teaser: American engineer who, in the summer of 1958, invented the integrated circuit — putting an entire circuit on a single chip of silicon — while his colleagues were on vacation. He shared the 2000 Nobel for the invention that made the computer age possible. Robert Noyce independently invented a similar chip months later, and the two fought over the patent for decades.

exploreAction.instruction: Read how Kilby, a new hire at Texas Instruments with no vacation time, worked alone in the empty lab and built a phase-shift oscillator on a single germanium chip — a circuit on one piece of semiconductor. He proved it to his boss on September 12, 1958. Today's chips hold billions of transistors. Noyce's version used silicon and won the market; the two inventors eventually shared credit and the patent war ended.

name: John Shriver
teaser: American chemist who, as a young scientist at DuPont, co-developed nylon 66 with Wallace Carothers in the 1930s — the first truly synthetic fiber — and helped scale it to commercial production. Nylon stockings, parachutes, and ropes transformed industry and the home. His work shows the quiet army of chemists behind every famous invention.

exploreAction.targetName: The DuPont nylon team's 1935–1939 development work
exploreAction.instruction: Read how the nylon project, led by Carothers but run by a team, moved from a lab curiosity to a commercial fiber in four years — inventing the drawing process that gives nylon its strength. Nylon stockings sold out in hours in 1940, and during WWII the fiber made parachutes and tire cord. The team's chemistry — condensing diamines with diacids — remains the basis of many synthetic fibers.

name: Alexander Grothendieck
teaser: French mathematician who rebuilt algebraic geometry from its foundations in the 1960s, creating a universe of abstract structures so powerful it solved problems that had stood for centuries — including Weil's conjectures. He won the Fields Medal in 1966, then abandoned mathematics and, later, society itself, living as a recluse in the Pyrenees until his death in 2014.

exploreAction.targetName: Grothendieck's EGA and SGA seminars and the solution of the Weil conjectures
exploreAction.instruction: Read how Grothendieck, rather than attacking problems directly, built vast new machinery — schemes, topologies, categories — that made the problems dissolve. His 1960s seminar notes run to thousands of pages and are still studied. He refused the 1966 Fields Medal ceremony to protest the Vietnam War, and later retreated from mathematics entirely, calling his work 'the wreck of my life.'

name: Pierre de Fermat
teaser: French lawyer and amateur mathematician who laid the foundations of number theory and probability, and who wrote in a book margin in 1637 that he had proved a 'marvelous' theorem that wouldn't fit — Fermat's Last Theorem, unsolved for 358 years until Andrew Wiles proved it in 1995. Fermat was a genius who published almost nothing.

exploreAction.targetName: Fermat's Last Theorem, the correspondence with Pascal on probability
exploreAction.instruction: Read the famous margin note in his copy of Arithmetica: 'I have discovered a truly marvelous proof of this, which this margin is too narrow to contain.' The theorem — no three positive integers satisfy aⁿ+bⁿ=cⁿ for n>2 — resisted every approach for three centuries, spawning vast new mathematics. Fermat and Pascal's 1654 letters on gambling founded probability theory. He died in 1665, his theorem unpublished.
